Complete Empirical Research Plan  

================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Preferred design: Two–stage least squares (instrumental‐variables, IV) that exploits plausibly exogenous weather shocks (rainfall and temperature deviations) as instruments for agricultural productivity.  

Why IV is appropriate  
• Rainfall and temperature in the growing season are orthogonal to households’ labor supply or wage‐setting decisions but strongly affect crop yields.  
• Annual household panel ⇒ we can difference out time‐invariant unobservables with household fixed effects and common macro trends with year (or region–year) fixed effects.  
• The IV approach directly delivers the local elasticity of wages with respect to productivity, which is the policy‐relevant parameter.  
Robustness / complementary designs:  
• Difference-in-differences & event-study specifications around large, discrete drought years as a validity check.  

================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable (endogenous regressor)  
 P_it ≡ log(agricultural output or yield) of household i in year t.  

Instrument(s)  
 Z_it ≡ standardized growing-season rainfall anomaly and growing-degree-days anomaly in the household’s district-crop-year.  

Control group / counterfactual  
 Households and years that experienced normal (within ±0.5 σ) rainfall/temperature. Because the design is continuous, they implicitly provide the counterfactual conditional on the fixed effects.  

Treatment timing  
 t is the agricultural year; weather shocks are observed before harvest, so their timing is well defined.  

No running variable or cutoff (not RDD).  

================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Relevance – Rainfall anomalies significantly move agricultural productivity.  
 Highly plausible; well documented agronomic relationship. We will report first-stage F-statistics (>10).  

A2. Exclusion – Conditional on fixed effects and controls, rainfall affects household wages only via its effect on agricultural productivity (no direct labor-market channel).  
 Plausible because the study is restricted to rural/agricultural households; nonetheless we include region-year FE to soak up any local labor-demand shocks caused directly by weather.  

A3. Monotonicity – More rainfall in deficit years never reduces productivity for treated households relative to controls (no “defiers”).  
 Reasonable given agronomic production functions for rain-fed crops.  

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value – Weather in one location does not affect wages of households in distant locations beyond the region FE.  
 Reasonable because labor markets are locally segmented; we cluster at district level.  

================================================================  
4. Main Threats & Mitigations  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Direct effect of rainfall on non-farm labor demand (violation of exclusion).  
 Mitigation: (i) include district–year fixed effects so identification comes from within-district crop mix differences; (ii) run placebo on purely non-agricultural wage earners—coefficient should be zero.  

T2. Migration or household composition changes following shocks ⇒ selection bias.  
 Mitigation: use balanced-panel households; control for household size & demographic composition; estimate intent‐to‐treat elasticities.  

T3. Measurement error in self-reported wages ⇒ attenuation bias.  
 Mitigation: instrument alleviates attenuation; further, winsorize extreme wage observations and re-estimate; triangulate with village-level wage data where available.  

================================================================  
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)      # fast data manipulation
library(fixest)          # high-performance FE + IV
library(modelsummary)    # nice tables

# 1. Load & merge data -----------------------------------------------------
hh  <- fread("household_panel.csv")          # household survey
wx  <- fread("weather_district_year.csv")    # rainfall & temp
geo <- fread("household_geo_lookup.csv")     # hh -> district

# merge
data <- merge(hh, geo, by = "hh_id")
data <- merge(data, wx, by = c("district_id","year"))

# 2. Construct variables ---------------------------------------------------
data[, rainfall_anom := (rainfall_gs - mean(rainfall_gs, na.rm = TRUE))/
                          sd(rainfall_gs,  na.rm = TRUE),
     by = district_id]

data[, gdd_anom      := (gdd_gs - mean(gdd_gs, na.rm = TRUE))/
                          sd(gdd_gs, na.rm = TRUE),
     by = district_id]

data[, log_prod  := log(ag_output + 1)]
data[, log_wage  := log(wage_rate)]

# 3. Main IV specification -------------------------------------------------
iv_formula <- log_wage ~ log_prod | . ~ rainfall_anom + gdd_anom

est_main <- feols(iv_formula,
                  data = data,
                  fixef = ~ hh_id + year,
                  cluster = "district_id")

# 4. First stage check -----------------------------------------------------
fs <- feols(log_prod ~ rainfall_anom + gdd_anom | hh_id + year,
            data = data, cluster = "district_id")

# 5. Robustness: difference-in-differences on drought years ---------------
data[, drought := as.integer(rainfall_anom <= -1)]
did_est <- feols(log_wage ~ drought * post |
                 hh_id + year, data = data,
                 cluster = "district_id")

# 6. Output ----------------------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(Main_IV = est_main, FirstStage = fs, DID = did_est),
             stars = TRUE)
```

================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Prior: Positive productivity shocks should raise local demand for agricultural labor and thus wages. Theory (short-run labor demand with inelastic land supply) suggests an elasticity of rural wages with respect to output of roughly +0.3. Therefore, a 10 % fall in output due to a rainfall shock should lower daily real wages by about 3 %.  

================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Strong first stage (F > 10) …… 1  
C2: Exclusion plausibility …………… 0.8  
C3: No heterogeneous direct effects …… 0.8  
C4: Correct functional form …………… 0.9  
C5: Appropriate clustering / inference … 1  

Total (average) validity score ≈ 0.9 → generally credible, but exclusion remains the key point to defend empirically.
